source: Softening a Collision
Stretching a collision over more time lowers the force, which is how airbags, helmets and crumple zones work.
Students think padding reduces the change in momentum, when it really spreads the same change over more time.

Drop an egg on a pillow and on a hard floor from the same height. It hits both at the same speed and stops in both cases, so its change in momentum is the same. Why does only one break? The answer combines momentum with the second law.
Force × time = change in momentum: $$F\,t = \Delta p \quad\text{so}\quad F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{t}$$ For the same change in momentum, a longer stopping time means a smaller force.

From $F = ma$ and $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{t}$, we get $F = \dfrac{m\,\Delta v}{t} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{t}$. The floor stops the egg in a tiny fraction of a second, so the force is huge. The pillow sinks in and takes many times longer, so the force is many times smaller.
The same ball stopped by a hard and a soft bumper. The soft bumper's force graph is lower and wider. The area under each graph, the change in momentum, is the same.
A 0.5 kg ball moving at 10 m/s is stopped by a wall in 0.01 s. Find the average force.
A hard stop
Change in momentum: $\Delta p = 0.5 \times 10 = 5$ kg·m/s.
The same ball is caught by a padded mitt that takes 0.1 s to stop it. Find the force.
A soft stop
Same $\Delta p = 5$ kg·m/s.
$F = \dfrac{5}{0.1} = 50$ N: ten times the time, one tenth the force.

Thinking padding reduces the change in momentum. The object must go from moving to stopped either way, so $\Delta p$ is the same. Padding, crumple zones and airbags spread that same change over more time, which lowers the force. Check: the speed before and after didn't change, so neither did $\Delta p$.
This is why a car's front end is built to crumple and why an airbag inflates: both stretch the stop over more time. A gymnast's mat and a catcher who pulls the glove back work the same way.
